claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced high-temperature ductility relative to commercially pure tungsten under plasma-facing-service loading conditions.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced high-temperature toughness relative to commercially pure tungsten under plasma-facing-service loading conditions.
Multicomponent lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr produces solid-solution strengthening.
Multicomponent lattice distortion raises the lattice friction stress and critical stress for dislocation glide.
The increased resistance to dislocation glide promotes dislocation storage and a high dislocation density.
Lattice distortion and the associated dislocation structure promote cross-slip-mediated plasticity.
Cross slip and dislocation storage delocalize plastic flow and distribute strain more homogeneously.
More homogeneous plastic flow reduces stress concentrations at crack tips.
Reduced crack-tip stress concentration suppresses cleavage and delays brittle fracture.
At 1000 °C, WTaTiVZr will have at least 50% greater uniform elongation than pure tungsten under the specified matched conditions.
At 1000 °C, WTaTiVZr will have at least 30% greater fracture toughness than pure tungsten under the specified matched conditions.
Pure tungsten has approximately 1% uniform elongation at 1000 °C under the stated test conditions.
Pure tungsten has fracture toughness of approximately 10 MPa·√m at 1000 °C under the stated test conditions.
The hypothesis applies from 900 to 1100 °C, at strain rates from 1×10^-4 to 1×10^-2 s^-1, in vacuum, and for grain sizes from 3 to 7 μm.
Matching WTaTiVZr and tungsten at approximately 5 μm grain size and testing them with identical loading and specimen geometry provides the proposed controlled comparison.
Failure to achieve both the specified elongation increase and toughness increase would falsify the stated quantitative hypothesis.
